extracted.intended_audience: literate early‑18th‑century reading public (coffee‑house readers, genteel society)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing moral/political periodical essays and social commentary in the style of The Spectator: how to observe society, frame reflections, and advance moral prescriptions. Also includes social‑moral maxims and aesthetic judgments (music, conduct, humour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against 'Platonick' love (friendship turning to passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A low opinion of 'Platonick Love' — friendships between the sexes, though called friendship, often 'improve Approbation into Kindness, and Kindness into Passion' and may conceal treacherous designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prolonged intimate intercourse between agreeable men and women when there is any risk of ambiguous attachments; the permission of such intercourse often converts successive fleeting passions into settled domestic arrangements and can lead to fatal consequences when friends of different sexes are too unanimous. Anti‑pattern: treating platonic friendship as morally safe when it can swell into physical passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public repentance must match public offence to repair reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a woman's jilting has been public, a private recantation will not suffice; as Philander says, 'unless you could contrive a way to make your Recantation as well known to the Publick, as they are already apprised of the manner with which you have treated me, you shall never more see Philander.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To restore social standing after a public wrong, make the reparation or apology equally public. Example: Amoret is advised to publish her repentance to recover Philander's favour; failing to do so will foreclose reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple local perspectives to understand public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a public matter one ought to 'hear the Reflections that arise upon it in the several Districts and Parishes of London and Westminster' — i.e. sample opinions across coffee‑houses and quarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: visit different coffee‑houses (St. James's, Giles's, Jenny Man's, Paul's Church‑Yard, Cheapside, etc.) and listen to the local 'statesman' of each to learn how the same event is framed by different social groups. Example: the same report (the French King's death) produces widely differing takes depending on patrons' interests and occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect news to be interpreted through private interest
rubrics_metrics.description: People naturally consider public events 'with a Regard to his own particular Interest and Advantage' — e.g., a fishmonger sees the death of a foreign king in terms of future mackerel supply, a banker in terms of stock sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reports or popular reaction, be sceptical of surface emotions: ask what private advantage or fear might shape each narrator's interpretation. Example anecdote: a haberdasher's confident prediction is undermined by incoming letters; his motive was reputation rather than information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Nature — choose pursuits aligned with innate talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature 'appoints every thing to a certain Use and Purpose' and 'Every Man has one or more Qualities which may make him useful'; excellence arises from following the bent given by nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select studies and professions that match one's natural disposition and gifts (oratory for Tully, poetry for Virgil). Anti‑pattern: abandoning natural talents to affect a different character (eg. Cleanthes aspiring to be a 'fine Gentleman'). Building on natural inclination is likened to 'laying the Foundation upon a Rock.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation — do not attempt characters one is not fit for
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation (seeking to excel in characters 'Men are not fit for') produces ridicule and moral disorder: coxcombs, false characters, and insipid productions arise from forcing oneself into unsuitable roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue arts, fashions, or public personae contrary to your genius; examples of anti‑patterns: Valerio (no genius for poetry but insists on writing verses), Cælia and Iras (each coveting the other's excellence), Semanthe (unnatural painting of her complexion). Result: loss of native excellence and acquisition of bad qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art cannot wholly substitute for nature; forced excellence is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: While art and contrivance may temporarily produce effects (like forcing a plant with a hotbed), they cannot supply the true seeds of moral or intellectual excellences that nature provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use education and practice to 'graft upon Nature' but do not expect skill alone to create genius where there is none. Anti‑pattern: expecting training to produce innate imaginative power or taste where natural inclination is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church music and sacred diction should draw on Scripture to elevate devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Composers should cultivate church music founded on 'Excellent Words' from the inspired Writings; Hebrew idioms and the diction of the Psalms give force, energy, and solemnity suited to divine songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for sacred music that 'improves our Virtue in proportion as it raised our Delight': set scriptural language to music, prefer Hebraic turns of phrase where appropriate, and use religious themes to purify and exalt the passions. Examples and authority: ancient practice (David composing odes and hymns), origin of the drama in religious chorus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as moral pedagogy — pleasure plus duty
rubrics_metrics.description: When music is properly applied to worship (hymns, anthems), 'Pleasure and Duty go hand in hand' — it strengthens devotion, produces lasting impressions, and purifies the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and programme music with moral ends: choose texts and melodies that produce 'more lasting and permanent Impressions' and encourage piety rather than transient sensual excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance solitude and public life; prefer a mixed, useful course
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremes of solitude or public life are faults: 'in the former Men generally grow useless by too much Rest, and in the latter are destroyed by too much Precipitation.' A mixt state (country and town) is most useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live as 'gentle Streams' that visit both lonely vales and populous towns; those naturally inclined to solitude should accept it, while those who can serve both should seek balance. Anti‑pattern: adopting an extreme posture that wastes faculties or destroys usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships between opposite sexes carry particular risks of resentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends who are of different sexes, when they fall out, often have resentments 'more keen than ever those of other Men can possibly be' and may suffer 'fatal Effects from their Unanimity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of cross‑sex intimacy and the expectation of complete openness; recognise the special emotional intensity and potential consequences of such friendships and manage them prudently to avoid social disaster.
